content.title: About
content.content: Brioche is a soft French bread made from wheat flour, eggs, butter, sugar and yeast. The dough is rich, slightly sweet, with a golden crust and a light, airy crumb. Brioche is often enjoyed at breakfast, as rolls, toast, or used in desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally brioche is shaped into a round loaf with a characteristic “crown” knot on top.
The original recipe uses a large amount of eggs, giving the bread its distinctive yellow hue.
Brioche is sometimes called the “royal bread” because it was served at French royal courts.
In the United States the “brioche bun” is popular for burgers and sandwiches.
Sweet versions may contain raisins, candied peel or chocolate chips.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rich in carbohydrates and fats, brioche quickly replenishes energy stores.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and yeast provide B1, B2, B3 and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Brioche supplies iron, magnesium and phosphorus, supporting blood and bone health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A modest amount of fiber from wheat flour aids normal digestion.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Tryptophan from eggs can help synthesize serotonin, the “feel‑good” hormone.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Brioche is rich in fats and sugars, so it should be eaten in moderation, especially for weight management.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional brioche contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet varieties can raise blood sugar levels, which is important for diabetics to consider.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs and butter add cholesterol, so those with high cholesterol should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brioche can be enjoyed fresh, toasted with butter, used in sandwiches, as a base for French toast, in bread pudding, or served with jam, honey and cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep brioche in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage freeze it in a bag – it will stay soft for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature or gently warm in the oven before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Mung beans (Vigna radiata) are small green legumes native to India and South Asia. They are eaten whole, split (dal), or as sprouts, and are also made into flour and starch. Mung beans have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor. They cook quickly and are widely used in the cuisines of India, China, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mung beans have been grown in South Asia for thousands of years.
Mung bean sprouts are a popular ingredient in Asian cooking, often called bean sprouts.
Mung bean starch is used to make clear glass noodles.
Mung beans cook faster than many other legumes and do not always need long soaking.
In Central Asia, mung beans are used in dishes such as mashhurda and mashkichiri.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Mung beans provide plant protein and are often used in plant-based diets.

items.title: Contain fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contain folate
items.content: Folate is important for cell formation.

items.title: Contain iron, magnesium, and potassium
items.content: These minerals support muscle and nerve function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Sprouts contain vitamin C
items.content: Mung bean sprouts are a light vegetable ingredient with vitamin C.

items.title: Raw sprouts
items.content: Raw sprouts can be contaminated with bacteria, so it is better to blanch or cook them; vulnerable people and pregnant women should avoid raw sprouts.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Like other legumes, mung beans can cause gas; soaking and introducing them gradually help.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Mung beans are legumes, and allergies are possible, including cross-reactions with other legumes.

items.title: Antinutrients
items.content: Raw mung beans contain phytates and lectins; soaking and thorough cooking reduce them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse mung beans, soak them for a few hours if you like, and cook for 20–30 minutes until soft; split mung beans cook faster. Add them to soups, porridges, pilaf, vegetable stews, and salads. Sprouts can be briefly blanched and added to salads and stir-fries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry mung beans in an airtight container in a dry, cool, dark place. Keep cooked mung beans in the refrigerator for 3–5 days. Store sprouts in the refrigerator and use them within a few days, as they spoil quickly.

pizza-with-extra-meat-thin-crust.title: Pizza with extra meat, thin crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with extra meat on a thin crust is a classic Italian pizza made with a crisp, thin dough, topped with tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and a generous assortment of meats: ham, sausage, bacon, and ground beef. Perfect for meat lovers seeking a hearty bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust bakes quickly and stays crunchy.
Extra meat is often a mix of several sausage types to enhance flavor complexity.
Traditional ovens bake pizza at 250‑300 °C, giving the crust a golden hue.
In Italy similar versions are called “pizza alla carne” and are served as a “speciale”.
Thin crust contains fewer calories than a thick crust, but the added meat keeps the overall calorie count high.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat toppings provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat and bacon are good sources of heme iron, helping prevent anemia.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Mozzarella supplies calcium, important for bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat ingredients are rich in B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene from tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes provide lycopene, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Meat and cheese can raise saturated fat intake, which may be undesirable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sausages and bacon are often salty, potentially contributing to elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A serving can exceed 800 kcal due to the abundance of meat and cheese.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Thin crust is typically made from wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into slices. For added freshness, top with raw vegetables such as arugula or cherry tomatoes after baking. Optional finishes include grated Parmesan or a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore the crust’s crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned lentil soup is a ready‑to‑eat soup made from whole red or green lentils, vegetables, spices and broth, sealed in an airtight can. It retains the nutritional qualities of lentils and is convenient for quick meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils are one of the oldest legume crops, cultivated for over 8,000 years.
Canning allows the soup to stay shelf‑stable for 2–3 years without added preservatives.
Lentil soup is considered a comfort food in many cultures, from Russia to India.
A typical can contains about 300–400 g of finished soup, ideal for a single serving on the go.
Lentils are rich in plant protein and iron, making them popular among vegetarians.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Lentils provide roughly 9 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and anemia prevention.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The soup contains minimal saturated fat, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Provides antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients in lentils help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often have added salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lentils.

items.title: Anti‑nutrients
items.content: Raw lentils contain phytic acid, but the canning process greatly reduces it.

items.title: Heat treatment
items.content: Heat the soup to a rolling boil to ensure any potential bacteria are destroyed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open the can, pour the contents into a pot and bring to a boil for 5–7 minutes. Add fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a drizzle of olive oil for extra flavor. The soup can be enjoyed on its own or as part of a larger meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer leftovers to an airtight container and keep refrigerated, consuming within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Spaghetti sauce with added vegetables is a ready‑to‑use tomato sauce enriched with carrots, celery, bell pepper and onion. It is designed for quick pasta preparation, giving the dish a rich flavor and an extra serving of vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce typically contains tomatoes, carrots, celery, onion and bell pepper, making it more nutritious than plain tomato sauce.
The vegetables are heat‑treated, preserving most of their vitamins and antioxidants.
It is popular in diet plans because it adds vegetables without the need to cook them separately.
Some versions include basil or oregano to boost aromatic notes.
The product can be ready‑to‑eat or require a brief heating before serving.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and skin.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Carrots and bell pepper supply beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes and pepper are good sources of vitamin C, aiding immune function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables helps maintain healthy gastrointestinal function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike creamy sauces, this product contains minimal fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions can be high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or other ingredients.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Industrial production may use preservatives; choose additive‑free options if preferred.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: A modest amount of sugar is sometimes added for balance; diabetics should take this into account.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the sauce in a saucepan or microwave, add it to cooked spaghetti and stir. It can also be used in lasagna, casseroles, as a pizza base, or as a dip for vegetable sticks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened sauce in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.
